Fragment of an official letter from Fustat addressed to a certain town in the Rīf (or perhaps a circular), exhorting them to be generous and assist the bearer with the payment of his capitation tax (five years' worth). For if they do not, he will go to prison for a long time, and it will be difficult to free him. Whatever money any town is able to raise on his behalf should not be given to the man himself, but rather the cantor of the town should send it to Fustat to the sender of this document. ASE
Literary. Eshkol ha-Kofer by Yehuda Hadasi. Dating: Possibly 15th or 16th c. Information from NLI.

Verso: Court record, written by Hillel b. Eli (fl. 1066–1108 CE), regarding a property in Qasr al-Sham'. One of the parties is a convert to Islam. The recto was reused for a letter ca. 1120 CE (PGPID 670).

Letter from a certain Bū l-Fatḥ "al-Malikī al-Kāmilī" to a distinguished physician. No details are preserved beyond the grand titles of the addressee. The sender may be identical with the Fatḥ al-Dīn who is known to have served as a supervisor of physicians under al-Malik al-Kāmil; see T-S AS 146.164 (PGPID 29072).

On verso there is additional text in Arabic script, maybe a preface to ethical exhortations (اسمع مني ما ا . . . . فهو من . . . .). Underneath there is part of the table of contents of a Judaeo-Arabic halakhic work: אלבאב אלתאלת עשר פי מא יתעלק באמר אלשמטה אלבאב אלראבע עשר פי מא

Lists of names in Judaeo-Arabic. Bifolium. Dating: Probably 13th or 14th century.

Accounts, listing weights and payments. Dating: 11th or 12th century. Hand of ʿArūs b. Yosef. Several of the accounts deal with silk. This fragment is likely a page from the same book of accounts as the neighboring shelfmark. Requires further examination.

Mentioning a variety of individuals, such as: Eliyahu Ṣahal, Aharon Ḥedef, Khalīfa Arūkh, Shelomo Sonina, Ḥayyīm Ḥazaq, Raḥamīm Ḥāmī, Barūkh Jazzār, among others. With further research, it may be possible to date the fragment based on the names listed (possibly early 19th-century?).
Note in Judaeo-Arabic informing the recipient that the bearer had a good reason for his tardiness this week, and please forgive him.
List of accounts, mentioning a wide variety of names and corresponding sums. Dated on the verso, in the first line of the second heading: 5 Kislev 5364 AM (1603 CE). Requires further examination.

Letter in Judaeo-Arabic. Unusual handwriting: blocky, calligraphic. The writer bemoans that he has lost all his money and merchandise. "The reason for the debt is that my work is with ... the Shaykh Abū Saʿd known as Abū [...]." The fragment ends around here. Probably he is going to ask for help.
Letter fragment in Judaeo-Arabic, with the address in Arabic script. Essentially unreadable without special imaging.
Letter fragment from Avraham אלגדיאני. In Hebrew and Judaeo-Arabic. Dating: 16th century. With greetings to Yosef al-Ashqar (see T-S NS 304.1 (PGPID 24958)).
Very faded and damaged, hardly legible, fragment from a legal query addresed to 'our Rabbis', regarding a quarell between two people and a payment of 15 dinars. On verso part of a draft of letter. AA

Recto: letter (to judge by the words من مولاي), three lines and the top half of a fourth from the right side. Cut and reused for the tiny letter on verso, starting with a cipher at the top and the basmala, then the usual opening formula كتبت لسيدي مولاي اطال الله بقاك and ending with the pre-closing formula ان شا الله.
Genesis.

Letter from Samḥūn b. Dāwūd ibn al-Siqillī (Qayrawān) to Yosef b. Yaʿaqov b. ʿAwkal (Fustat). The letter deals with a conflict between the sender and the recipient over a consignment of brazilwood, which Samḥūn b. Daʿūd sent to Spain against the instructions of Yosef b. ʿAwkal. This caused a delay in payments and a break of contact between the two. (Information from Gil, Kingdom, Vol. 2, p. 644.)

Some of the paper layers are very fibrous. This format gives off the appearance of cardboard, but may be an unintentional result of high compression in the geniza chamber from the collective weight of its contents. Early modern legal fragment in Hebrew. The paleography points to the likelihood that the document is c. 17th-19th-century. Based on the limited text available this fragment may trace back to a real estate rental or purchase concerning a shop (חנות). The term ההקדש (ha-heqdesh) is used in line 8 and perhaps line 3 in connection with this shop property. A sum of 25 grosho is listed but it's unclear if this term indicates Ottoman kuruş or just a generic term for silver coinage. The name Avraham ʿAfīf appears in line 2. MCD.

Khalīfa in the city of Mosul in the year 5521 AM = 1760/61 CE. Verso contains possibly a different letter as well as the end of a legal deed about a geṭ, at 90 degrees. Needs examination.

tags: jamakiyya, government officials, bimaristan, Fatimid, physician, Petition
desc:
Petition in Arabic script from a physician employed in the hospital in Cairo who had a government stipend of 5 dinars per month. This stipend has evidently been threatened, so he writes this petition to ensure that he will continue to get it. Alternatively, he has been promised the stipend but hasn't actually started to receive it yet. The formulary suggests 12th-century Fatimid origin. Instead of جملة in l. 2 it is also possible to read جمكية (jāmakiyya, "stipend," though this is typically spelled with an alif).

Legal record (#100) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 33v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). David ha-Ḥazzan Fayrūz agrees to make monetary contributions to the pious endowment that are earmarked based on him receiving the synagogue honors of three years ʿaliyot for Torah readings. For another early modern document regarding charitable contributions and synagogue honors, see: Moss. IXa,3.20 (PGPID 26885). MCD.

On verso there are jottings in both Arabic script and Judaeo-Arabic, perhaps describing recto (כלמה שכתב מרנו . . . הדיין המופלא . . . נמשול).

Very long letter dated ca. 1100, issued by the two judges of the capital in the name of the Nagid Mevorakh, in which a circuit judge is strongly rebuked for having given judgment in a town in the absence of the local muqaddam and for having taken other actions without consulting him and the elders. (Information from Mediterranean Society, II, pp. 74, 537)
